theorySlides.title: JOINs 🔗
theorySlides.content:
Combine rows from multiple tables:
• **INNER JOIN**: Matching rows only
• **LEFT JOIN**: All left + matching right
• **RIGHT JOIN**: All right + matching left
• **FULL JOIN**: All from both

theorySlides.title: INNER JOIN
theorySlides.content: Get matching records from both tables.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
SELECT users.name, orders.total
FROM users
INNER JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id;

-- Only users WITH orders

theorySlides.title: RIGHT & FULL JOIN 🔄
theorySlides.content:
More JOIN types:
• **RIGHT JOIN**: All right table rows + matching left
• **FULL OUTER JOIN**: All rows from both tables
• NULL fills missing matches
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- RIGHT JOIN: All orders, even without users
SELECT users.name, orders.total
FROM users
RIGHT JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id;

-- FULL JOIN: All users AND all orders
SELECT users.name, orders.total
FROM users
FULL OUTER JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id;

theorySlides.title: Multiple JOINs 🔗🔗
theorySlides.content:
Chain multiple tables together:
• Join as many tables as needed
• Each JOIN adds more data
• Order matters for readability
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
SELECT 
  u.name,
  o.order_date,
  p.product_name,
  oi.quantity
FROM users u
INNER JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
INNER JOIN order_items oi ON o.id = oi.order_id
INNER JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.id;

theorySlides.title: Self JOIN 🪞
theorySlides.content:
Join a table to itself:
• Useful for hierarchical data
• Compare rows in same table
• Must use table aliases
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Find employees and their managers
SELECT 
  e.name AS employee,
  m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;

-- Find pairs of users from same city
SELECT a.name, b.name, a.city
FROM users a
JOIN users b ON a.city = b.city AND a.id < b.id;

questions.question: Which JOIN includes all left table rows?
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from left table.

questions.question: What does FULL OUTER JOIN return?
questions.explanation: FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, with NULL for non-matching rows.

questions.question: When would you use a self JOIN?
options: To find hierarchical relationships in same table
questions.explanation: Self JOINs are useful for hierarchical data like employees/managers or finding relationships within the same table.

questions.question: How many tables can you JOIN in one query?
questions.explanation: You can chain as many JOINs as needed, though performance may decrease with many tables.

theorySlides.title: Subqueries 📦
theorySlides.content:
A query nested inside another query.

Useful for:
• Filtering with computed values
• Creating temp result sets
• Complex conditions

theorySlides.title: Example
theorySlides.content: Find above-average salaries.

theorySlides.title: IN Subquery 📋
theorySlides.content:
Check if value exists in a list:
• Returns TRUE if value matches any result
• Alternative to multiple OR conditions
• Can use NOT IN for exclusion

theorySlides.title: EXISTS Subquery ✅
theorySlides.content:
Check if subquery returns any rows:
• Returns TRUE/FALSE
• Often faster than IN
• Use for existence checks

theorySlides.title: Correlated Subqueries 🔄
theorySlides.content:
Subquery references outer query:
• Executes once per outer row
• More powerful but slower
• Uses outer table aliases
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Find employees earning more than dept average
SELECT name, salary, department_id
FROM employees e1
WHERE salary > (
  SELECT AVG(salary)
  FROM employees e2
  WHERE e2.department_id = e1.department_id
);

-- Find latest order per customer
SELECT * FROM orders o1
WHERE order_date = (
  SELECT MAX(order_date) FROM orders o2
  WHERE o2.customer_id = o1.customer_id
);

questions.question: Where can subqueries appear?
questions.explanation: Subqueries can be in SELECT, FROM, or WHERE clauses.

questions.question: What does EXISTS return?
questions.explanation: EXISTS returns TRUE if the subquery returns any rows, FALSE otherwise.

questions.question: What is a correlated subquery?
options: A subquery that references the outer query
questions.explanation: A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query and executes once per outer row.

questions.question: When is EXISTS often better than IN?
options: When checking if rows exist (not values)
questions.explanation: EXISTS can be faster because it stops as soon as it finds a match, while IN evaluates all values.

theorySlides.title: Grouping Data 📊
theorySlides.content:
GROUP BY groups rows for aggregation.

HAVING filters groups (like WHERE for aggregates).

Order: WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY

theorySlides.title: Example
theorySlides.content: Find categories with high sales.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
SELECT category, SUM(amount) as total
FROM sales
GROUP BY category
HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000
ORDER BY total DESC;

theorySlides.title: Multiple Column Grouping 📊📊
theorySlides.content:
Group by multiple columns:
• Creates unique combinations
• More granular aggregation
• Order of columns matters
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Sales by category AND year
SELECT 
  category,
  YEAR(sale_date) as year,
  SUM(amount) as total,
  COUNT(*) as num_sales
FROM sales
GROUP BY category, YEAR(sale_date)
ORDER BY category, year;

-- Result: Electronics 2023 5000, Electronics 2024 7000...

theorySlides.title: HAVING with Multiple Conditions 🎯
theorySlides.content:
Filter groups with complex conditions:
• Use AND/OR in HAVING
• Can combine multiple aggregates
• Filter after grouping
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Categories with high sales AND many orders
SELECT 
  category,
  SUM(amount) as total,
  COUNT(*) as orders
FROM sales
GROUP BY category
HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000 
   AND COUNT(*) >= 10;

-- Customers with avg order > 100 but < 500
SELECT customer_id, AVG(total) as avg_order
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING AVG(total) BETWEEN 100 AND 500;

theorySlides.title: WHERE + GROUP BY + HAVING 🔗
theorySlides.content:
Combine all clauses effectively:
• WHERE: Filter rows BEFORE grouping
• GROUP BY: Create groups
• HAVING: Filter groups AFTER aggregation
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- 2024 sales by category, only categories > 5000
SELECT 
  category,
  SUM(amount) as total
FROM sales
WHERE sale_date >= '2024-01-01'   -- Filter rows first
GROUP BY category                  -- Then group
HAVING SUM(amount) > 5000          -- Filter groups
ORDER BY total DESC;

-- Active customers with many orders
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) as orders
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

questions.question: Difference between WHERE and HAVING?
options: WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups
questions.explanation: WHERE filters before grouping, HAVING after.

questions.question: What happens when you GROUP BY multiple columns?
options: Creates unique combinations of all columns
questions.explanation: GROUP BY multiple columns creates a group for each unique combination of values.

questions.question: Can you use WHERE and HAVING in the same query?
questions.explanation: Yes! WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

questions.question: Which is correct execution order?
questions.explanation: SQL executes: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY.

theorySlides.title: Window Functions 🪟
theorySlides.content:
Perform calculations across rows:
• ROW_NUMBER(): Sequential number
• RANK(): Rank with gaps
• LAG/LEAD: Previous/next row
• SUM() OVER: Running total

theorySlides.title: Example
theorySlides.content: Rank employees by salary.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
SELECT 
  name,
  salary,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) as rank
FROM employees;

-- Result: Alex 100k #1, Bob 80k #2...

theorySlides.title: LAG & LEAD Functions ⏮️⏭️
theorySlides.content:
Access previous/next row values:
• **LAG()**: Get value from previous row
• **LEAD()**: Get value from next row
• Great for comparisons and trends
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
SELECT 
  sale_date,
  amount,
  LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) as prev_amount,
  LEAD(amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) as next_amount,
  amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) as change
FROM sales;

-- Result: Shows each sale with previous and next amounts

theorySlides.title: Running Totals 📈
theorySlides.content:
Calculate cumulative sums:
• SUM() OVER with ORDER BY
• Running count, avg also possible
• Resets with PARTITION BY
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
SELECT 
  order_date,
  amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) as running_total,
  COUNT(*) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) as order_num,
  AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) as running_avg
FROM orders;

-- Running total per customer
SELECT customer_id, order_date, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (
    PARTITION BY customer_id 
    ORDER BY order_date
  ) as customer_running_total
FROM orders;

theorySlides.title: PARTITION BY Examples 📊
theorySlides.content:
Divide data into groups for calculations:
• Like GROUP BY but keeps all rows
• Each partition calculated separately
• Combine with any window function
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Rank employees within each department
SELECT 
  name,
  department,
  salary,
  RANK() OVER (
    PARTITION BY department 
    ORDER BY salary DESC
  ) as dept_rank
FROM employees;

-- Percentage of department total
SELECT 
  name,
  department,
  salary,
  salary * 100.0 / SUM(salary) OVER (
    PARTITION BY department
  ) as pct_of_dept
FROM employees;

questions.question: What does PARTITION BY do?
questions.explanation: PARTITION BY divides rows into groups for window calculations.

questions.question: What does LAG() return?
questions.explanation: LAG() returns the value from the previous row in the result set.

questions.question: How do you calculate a running total?
questions.explanation: SUM() OVER with ORDER BY calculates a running total that accumulates row by row.

questions.question: Difference between ROW_NUMBER and RANK?
questions.explanation: RANK gives same number to ties and skips next numbers. ROW_NUMBER is always sequential.

theorySlides.title: Database Indexes ⚡
theorySlides.content:
Indexes speed up queries:
• Like book index - fast lookup
• Create on frequently queried columns
• Trade-off: Slower writes, more storage

theorySlides.title: Creating Indexes
theorySlides.content: Index common search columns.

theorySlides.title: Composite Indexes 🔗
theorySlides.content:
Index multiple columns together:
• Column order matters!
• Leftmost columns used first
• Great for multi-column WHERE/ORDER BY

theorySlides.title: EXPLAIN Analyze 🔍
theorySlides.content:
Understand query execution:
• Shows if index is used
• Reveals full table scans
• Helps optimize slow queries
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
-- Basic EXPLAIN
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'test@example.com';

-- Shows: type, possible_keys, key, rows scanned

-- EXPLAIN ANALYZE (actual execution)
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders 
WHERE customer_id = 100 AND status = 'pending';

-- Look for:
-- ✅ "Using index" - Good!
-- ❌ "Full table scan" - Needs index
-- ❌ "filesort" - Consider index on ORDER BY

theorySlides.title: Index Best Practices 📋
theorySlides.content:
When to use indexes:
• Columns in WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY
• High cardinality columns (many unique values)
• Foreign keys

Avoid indexes on:
• Frequently updated columns
• Small tables
• Low cardinality (few unique values)

questions.question: When NOT to use indexes?
questions.explanation: Frequent updates slow down with indexes due to maintenance.

questions.question: In composite index (A, B, C), which queries use it?
options: WHERE A, WHERE A+B, WHERE A+B+C
Any combination of A, B, C
questions.explanation: Composite indexes work left-to-right. Queries must include leftmost columns to use the index.

questions.question: What does EXPLAIN help you find?
options: Query execution plan and index usage
questions.explanation: EXPLAIN shows how the database executes a query, including which indexes are used.

questions.question: What is "cardinality" in index context?
questions.explanation: Cardinality is the number of unique values. High cardinality columns (many unique values) benefit most from indexes.
